name: Reader-LM and model-based HTML-to-markdown. Covers Jina AI's reader-lm-0.5b and reader-lm-1.5b (Sept 2024) and their successor ReaderLM-v2 (Feb 2025, arXiv:2503.01151), plus the general question of a small decoder-only LM performing HTML->markdown as a learned selective-copy transduction rather than a rule-based or classifier-driven extraction. Aliases: readerlm-v2, jinaai/ReaderLM-v2, jinaai/reader-lm-1.5b, jinaai/reader-lm-0.5b; exposed commercially as the `x-engine: readerlm-v2` header on Jina's r.jina.ai Reader API.
kind: Model-based extraction/serialization approach: an open-weight small language model (research result with a production API wrapper), not a standard, benchmark, or regulation. Evaluated here as a candidate extraction/serialization stage, in direct tension with this project's deterministic, structure-agnostic fold.
maturity: Production-adjacent but young and actively revised. reader-lm v1 (0.5B/1.5B) shipped Sept 2024; ReaderLM-v2 shipped Feb 2025 as a full retrain (new data pipeline, new decoding strategy) rather than a fine-tune, which is itself evidence the v1 approach needed structural fixes, not just more data. Both generations are shipped as Hugging Face weights (Apache derivative repos exist for GGUF/quantized variants from third parties) and as a hosted Jina API engine. No version has an independent long-run production track record comparable to Trafilatura's decade of use; the arXiv paper for v2 is a company technical report, not a peer-reviewed publication.
license: CC-BY-NC-4.0 on both generations (Hugging Face model cards for jinaai/reader-lm-1.5b and jinaai/ReaderLM-v2; Jina's own Feb 2025 announcement post states the same). Non-commercial use only under the stated licence terms; commercial use requires contacting Jina AI directly. This is a hard blocker for any commercial deployment of this project without a separate agreement, independent of the technical fit question. [uncertain] whether Jina offers a standard commercial licence path or only case-by-case.
keeps_and_discards:
Unlike every heuristic/classifier extractor in this item set, a Reader-LM does not have a 'discards' policy in the normal sense -- it is trained to reproduce main content faithfully as a copy-with-reformatting task, and its failure mode is not selective omission but generative drift: it can both drop content that was present and add content that was never present. The v2 paper's own headline metric (ROUGE-L 0.84-0.86 depending on the reported table, on the vendor's WebMarkdown-1M-derived test set) means roughly 14-16% of n-gram overlap is already lost relative to a reference on the vendor's own easiest framing of the task. The publicly documented worst case is qualitatively different from anything else in this item set: a user feeding reader-lm-v2 (via Ollama) the two-sentence German snippet `

Hallo Welt

Schön, dass du hier bist

` got back a fabricated biography of a fictional web designer named 'Markus' with invented credentials, portfolio links and project descriptions -- content with zero basis in the four-word input (GitHub, ollama/ollama issue #6875, filed as a bug, no maintainer explanation or resolution recorded at time of research). That is not a discard/keep tradeoff, it is confabulation, and it is the central reason this class of tool is treated differently from every rule-based extractor in this project's item list.
structure_preserved: When it works, structure preservation is Reader-LM's strongest selling point relative to heuristic extractors: Jina's own comparisons and a third-party heuristic-vs-ML writeup (contextractor.com, 'Trafilatura vs. Jina ReaderLM') both report that ReaderLM-v2 is materially better than Trafilatura-class tools at preserving tables, nested lists, and other rich Markdown structure that density-heuristic extractors tend to flatten into plain paragraphs. That advantage is inseparable from the same generative mechanism that produces the hallucination failure mode above: the model is not literally copying substrings, it is generating tokens conditioned on the HTML, so 'better structure' and 'invented structure' are two expressions of the same underlying non-copy behaviour. Shadow DOM and closed roots are entirely out of scope -- the model consumes serialized HTML text handed to it and has no DOM/shadow awareness at all; whatever the sensor already flattened into that HTML string is all it can see.
interactive_elements: Controls survive only as whatever HTML markup happens to render into Markdown-expressible form (e.g. a checkbox's checked attribute may or may not survive as literal text depending on how the model was trained to handle non-content attributes -- this is not documented at attribute granularity in either the v1 blog post or the v2 paper). There is no dedicated interactive-element handling; the model was trained on 'HTML -> clean Markdown/JSON' pairs, and Markdown itself has no native representation for most interactive semantics, so most of it is lost by the target format before the model even enters the picture.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not addressed in either publication and not something Markdown as an output format can represent well regardless of the model. Disabled/checked/selected/expanded/aria states are not evaluated, not benchmarked, and structurally likely to be either dropped or (per the hallucination finding above) fabricated under uncertainty, since the model has no mechanism to say 'I don't know' about an attribute it wasn't trained to reproduce -- it will generate its best-guess token sequence regardless. This is the field where the accessibility-tree-vs-markdown gap that project's own fields.yaml calls out is sharpest, and a generative Markdown model does not close that gap; it inherits Markdown's representational poverty and adds sampling noise on top.
layout_awareness: None. Reader-LM operates purely on serialized HTML/text; it has no notion of rendered geometry, computed style, or visibility. This is a point of alignment with the project's no_layout_in_the_fold constraint at the input side, but it is also exactly why the model cannot filter concealed content (display:none, aria-hidden, off-screen positioning) any better than the raw HTML lets it -- and unlike a deterministic fold, when the model is uncertain about what a chunk of markup means, it can render it as if it were visible content, or omit it, unpredictably.
javascript_required: No -- the model consumes already-serialized HTML as text input; it does not execute anything and has no opinion about whether the HTML came from a live rendered DOM, a static fetch, or a cached snapshot. Whatever produced that HTML string (a headless browser, a plain HTTP fetch) determines whether JS-rendered content is present in the input at all; the model is downstream of that decision entirely.
evaluation_method: Vendor-run automatic-metric evaluation in both generations, supplemented by vendor-run qualitative scoring in v1. v1 (Sept 2024 blog post): ROUGE-L, Token Error Rate (TER, defined by Jina as the fraction of hallucinated tokens not present in the source HTML) and Word Error Rate (WER, insertions+substitutions+deletions), plus a 1-5 qualitative rubric across four dimensions (header extraction, main-content extraction, rich-structure preservation, Markdown syntax usage) scored over 22 hand-picked HTML sources in English, German, Japanese and Chinese -- a small, non-random, vendor-selected qualitative set. v2 (arXiv:2503.01151): character-level metrics (Levenshtein, Damerau-Levenshtein) and sequence metrics (ROUGE-L, Jaro-Winkler) for Markdown; for JSON extraction, tree-structured precision/recall/F1/pass-rate. No published study in either generation uses a held-out, independently-curated benchmark that the model's own authors did not construct; the one independent comparison found in this research (WCXB, arXiv:2605.21097) evaluates ReaderLM-v2 on a benchmark built by a different team for a different purpose (boilerplate removal, not Markdown fidelity) and reports it losing to heuristic extractors -- see reported_precision_recall and evidence_independence below.
corpus_size_and_origins: v1: no fixed named test corpus size is given beyond the 22-source qualitative set; the training data is 2.5B tokens (1.5B tokens at up to 32K sequence length, 1.2B tokens at up to 128K) drawn from Jina Reader API output pairs plus GPT-4o-synthesized data -- origins of the underlying URLs are not enumerated. v2: trained on 'WebMarkdown-1M', 1 million web pages drawn from the top 500 Common Crawl domains (so a large but domain-concentrated pool -- top-500-domain traffic skews toward large, well-formed commercial/media sites, not the long tail), with English (62.7%) and Chinese (~20%) accounting for over 80% of the set combined; average document length ~56,000 tokens. The held-out test set actually used for the headline v2 numbers is much smaller: 500 HTML-to-Markdown documents and 300 HTML-to-JSON documents, manually verified -- and both are drawn from the same WebMarkdown-1M distribution, so it is an in-distribution test set, not an independent corpus. The one cross-corpus data point available is WCXB's 2,008 pages from 1,613 distinct origins (dev 1,497 / held-out test 511) across 7 structural page types -- a materially larger and more origin-diverse corpus than either Reader-LM publication's own test set, and it is not the corpus the vendor numbers were computed on.
reported_precision_recall: Multiple, partially inconsistent, self-reported number sets, each over a different vendor-controlled test set, plus one independent contradicting result. v1 (22-source qualitative set / own blog): reader-lm-1.5b ROUGE-L 0.72, WER 1.87, TER 0.19; reader-lm-0.5b ROUGE-L 0.56, WER 3.28, TER 0.34; comparison baselines on the same set -- GPT-4o ROUGE-L 0.43/WER 5.88/TER 0.50, Gemini-1.5-Pro 0.42/3.16/0.48, LLaMA-3.1-70B 0.40/9.87/0.50, Gemini-1.5-Flash 0.40/21.70/0.55. v2 (WebMarkdown-1M test set, 500 docs / arXiv paper and HF model card, values differ slightly by which table is quoted): ROUGE-L 0.84-0.86, Levenshtein distance 0.20-0.22, Jaro-Winkler 0.82-0.83, versus GPT-4o ROUGE-L 0.69/Levenshtein 0.40/Jaro-Winkler 0.75 on the same set (a reported 24.6% ROUGE-L improvement over GPT-4o); JSON extraction F1 0.81, precision 0.82, recall 0.81, pass-rate 0.98-0.99. Independent contradiction: a secondary write-up of the WCXB benchmark (arXiv:2605.21097, corpus described above) states ReaderLM-v2 scores F1 0.741 on WCXB's boilerplate-removal task, below top heuristic systems, with rs-trafilatura reported at F1 0.859 while running orders of magnitude faster (~44 ms/page cited for rs-trafilatura versus a GPU-bound multi-second-per-page generation cost for ReaderLM-v2). [uncertain] -- this WCXB comparison number was read from a third-party blog's characterization of the paper (contextractor.com) rather than extracted directly from the WCXB PDF tables, which this research could not fully render (the fetched PDF came back password-protected on re-read); treat the 0.741/0.859 figures as directionally credible but not independently re-verified against the primary table.
independent_oracle: Weak. Neither reader-lm generation publishes an evaluation run by a party without a stake in the model's success, and TER/WER/ROUGE-L against a reference Markdown string are themselves generated by the same synthesis pipeline (Draft-Refine-Critique, itself LLM-based) that produced the training data, so the metric and the model share upstream assumptions about what 'clean Markdown' looks like. The one arguably independent check is WCXB, built by a different team for a different benchmark purpose and evaluating ReaderLM-v2 as one of 13 systems rather than as the paper's subject -- that is the closest thing to an independent oracle this research found, and it disagrees with the vendor's own numbers in direction (heuristics ahead, not behind).
evidence_independence: Predominantly vendor-produced. Every headline number above except the WCXB figure comes from Jina AI's own blog posts, model cards, or arXiv technical report -- the same pattern the fields.yaml documentation already flags as endemic to HTML-to-markdown comparisons generally ('nearly all current HTML-to-markdown comparisons are vendor-run and mutually contradictory'), and this item is a clean instance of exactly that problem: the v1 and v2 papers report different ROUGE-L values (0.72 vs 0.84-0.86) on different self-constructed test sets against different baseline sets, so the two generations are not even comparable to each other on their own published numbers, let alone to a third party's.
page_archetype_coverage: Not reported by either Reader-LM publication -- no per-archetype (article/forum/product/listing/documentation/service) breakdown exists in the vendor materials, only an aggregate score over the vendor's own test distribution (which itself skews toward the top-500-Common-Crawl-domain population that produced its training data). WCXB is the only source in this research with genuine per-archetype numbers, and it reports the general pattern this project's other items already cite: near-ceiling performance on articles (F1 ~0.93 for the field generally) but a sharp drop on structured page types (0.41-0.84 range) -- with no ReaderLM-v2-specific per-archetype number available from what could be fetched here. Given WCXB's aggregate placement of ReaderLM-v2 below the heuristic leaders, and given that generative models are plausibly worse, not better, on the highly repetitive DOM patterns of listing/product pages (the same 'thousands of near-identical sibling subtrees' pattern the Patricia-trie item in this set flags as a structural worst case), the prior should be that ReaderLM-v2's archetype spread is at least as wide as the heuristics', not narrower. [uncertain].
script_and_locale_behaviour: Both generations claim multilingual support: v1 was qualitatively evaluated on English, German, Japanese and Chinese; v2's base is Qwen2.5, which Jina's materials describe as covering 29 languages, and the WebMarkdown-1M training corpus is dominated by English (62.7%) and Chinese (~20%), with all other languages sharing the remaining ~17%. That skew means claimed multilingual coverage is unevenly evidenced -- the two dominant training languages are far better represented than the other 27 claimed languages, and no per-language accuracy breakdown is published for any of them. Nothing in either publication addresses RTL scripts, CJK punctuation edge cases, or whitespace-free segmentation specifically; a generative model's greater vulnerability here (versus a rule-based extractor) is that a script it under-saw in training is exactly the condition under which its confabulation failure mode (see keeps_and_discards) is most likely to trigger, since the model must generate plausible-looking output even when its internal confidence should be low, and nothing in the architecture surfaces that low confidence to the caller.
leaks_outward: Depends entirely on deployment mode, and the two modes have very different privacy postures that the vendor material does not clearly separate. Self-hosted (open weights via Hugging Face/GGUF, run locally e.g. under Ollama): no outward disclosure beyond whatever the local inference stack itself does; the model performs no network calls. Hosted (Jina's r.jina.ai Reader API with `x-engine: readerlm-v2`): the full page content and, implicitly, the URL being read, are sent to Jina's servers for processing, which is a materially different disclosure profile from every purely local extractor in this project's other items (Readability, Trafilatura, Resiliparse all run in-process). Any adoption of the hosted path would need its own privacy review; the open-weight path avoids the issue entirely.
mechanism_detectability: Not detectable by the target page under either deployment mode, in the sense this field's description means (attachShadow patching, CDP Runtime.enable, extension presence, timing side channels) -- the model consumes already-captured HTML/text and has no live relationship to the page being read, so it adds no detection surface beyond whatever captured the HTML in the first place. This is a genuine point of alignment with a stealthy sensor design: the choice of what post-processes captured markup is invisible to the origin regardless of whether that post-processor is a regex, a heuristic classifier, or an LLM.
countermeasures: Not applicable as a defensive category in the usual sense (there is no adversary detecting the technique), but there is a countermeasure the model itself needed against its own instability: v2's training added a contrastive loss specifically to suppress the 'dull loop' repetitive-token degeneration observed in v1, where the model would enter a repetition cycle and stop decoding early; v1 also used contrastive search decoding plus an explicit repetition stop criterion as inference-time mitigations. These are countermeasures against the model's own failure modes, not against any external detector, and their existence is itself evidence of how unstable base autoregressive generation is for this task without explicit intervention.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured as a hardening tradeoff in the project's sense (there is no privacy-hardening step being traded against fidelity here), but the closest analogous number is the cost of choosing model-based extraction over a heuristic baseline at all: WCXB's independently-reported F1 gap (ReaderLM-v2 0.741 vs rs-trafilatura 0.859, both against the same benchmark, if the secondary source is accurate) is a measured fidelity cost of roughly 12 F1 points for adopting the generative approach, paid in exchange for the structural-preservation gains noted under structure_preserved -- and paid alongside a large speed cost (GPU-bound generation vs rs-trafilatura's cited ~44ms/page).
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented or discussed in either publication. As with every extractor in this item set, gate state (consent banner, paywall, login wall, CAPTCHA) is a property of the capture pipeline feeding the model, not of the model itself; Reader-LM has no mechanism to detect or record it, and inherits whatever HTML the browser/fetch layer handed it, gated or not.
determinism: Not deterministic by default, and this is a categorical difference from every non-LLM extractor in this project's item set. Autoregressive decoding with sampling (temperature, contrastive search) means the same HTML input can produce different Markdown output on repeated runs unless the caller pins a fully greedy/deterministic decoding configuration and a fixed random seed, and even then, floating-point non-associativity across different GPU hardware or batch sizes can change results at the margin -- a well-known property of transformer inference generally, not documented as specifically characterized for Reader-LM in either publication. Where a rule-based extractor's determinism is a design property, a Reader-LM's determinism is a configuration choice the operator must actively make and verify.
determinism_across_versions: Poor by the clearest available evidence: v1 and v2 are not the same model incrementally updated but a full retrain with a new data pipeline (Draft-Refine-Critique) and new decoding strategy, and their own self-reported ROUGE-L numbers on their respective self-constructed test sets are not comparable (0.72 for v1-1.5b vs 0.84-0.86 for v2) because the underlying test distributions differ. Any project depending on Reader-LM output as a stable artifact must expect a model upgrade to change output distribution non-trivially and without a migration path, unlike a browser-version-driven xpath drift (the Patricia-trie item's determinism_across_versions concern) which is at least incremental and traceable to specific parser changes.
reproducibility: Weak for the model's own outputs (see determinism above) and further weakened by the training data itself: WebMarkdown-1M's construction (crawled from Common Crawl's top 500 domains) is not published as a frozen, versioned, redistributable dataset artifact in the fetched materials, so even re-deriving the vendor's own benchmark numbers from scratch is not straightforwardly possible for a third party. The model weights themselves are versioned and pinned on Hugging Face, which is the one genuinely reproducible axis -- a specific commit of jinaai/ReaderLM-v2 will behave identically given identical input and decoding configuration.
failure_modes: Four documented, and they are qualitatively different in kind from every rule-based extractor here. (1) CONFABULATION -- generating content with no basis in the source input, up to and including entire fabricated biographical narratives from a four-word HTML snippet (ollama/ollama #6875); this is not an edge case reported once but a structurally expected consequence of generative decoding under distributional uncertainty. (2) REPETITIVE DEGENERATION / DULL LOOPS -- the model enters a repetition cycle and stops decoding early, addressed but not eliminated by contrastive decoding and an explicit stop criterion (both publications). (3) LENGTH-DEPENDENT COPY FAILURE -- Jina's own v1 writeup states models under 360M parameters could only achieve 'reasonable copy behavior' on sequences under 1K tokens, implying copy fidelity is itself parameter- and length-dependent rather than guaranteed at any size; nothing in either publication states a token length past which even the 1.5B model's copy fidelity is no longer reliable. (4) TRAINING-BOUNDARY CORRUPTION -- v1's writeup mentions hallucination linked to examples split across sequence boundaries during data packing, i.e. an artifact of how training examples were chunked, which is a training-pipeline failure mode rather than an inference-time one and gives no guarantee it cannot recur in future training runs.
failure_visibility: Silent by construction, and worse than every rule-based extractor in this item set on this specific axis. A heuristic extractor that misclassifies a region produces recognizably wrong output (a nav bar included, a paragraph dropped) that is often visually or structurally obvious; a generative model's confabulated output is specifically optimized (by the training objective) to look like plausible, well-formed Markdown, which makes silent failure harder to detect by inspection, not easier. No confidence score, per-token provenance signal, or copy-vs-generate flag is exposed by either publication -- the model gives no signal distinguishing 'this text was copied from the source' from 'this text was generated because the model was uncertain what belonged here'. This is a direct and serious violation of the project's stated no-silent-degradation preference.
scale_limits: Two distinct scale axes, both documented. (a) SEQUENCE LENGTH: v1 supports up to 256K tokens context; v2 is trained progressively to 256K and claims extrapolation to 512K combined input+output via zigzag-ring-attention and an increased RoPE base frequency (5,000,000) -- but a claimed extrapolation ceiling is not the same as a measured-fidelity ceiling, and neither publication reports whether fidelity (ROUGE-L, TER) degrades as documents approach that ceiling; the 56,000-token average document length in the training corpus is well below either stated maximum, so the high end of the claimed range is largely untested territory by the vendor's own reported evaluation. (b) COMPUTE/THROUGHPUT: the HF model card's own T4-GPU figures (67 tokens/s input, 36 tokens/s output, and a caveat that T4 lacks bf16/flash-attention-2 support, further increasing memory use and slowing inference) put a single-page conversion at multiple seconds to potentially tens of seconds depending on document length and hardware, several orders of magnitude slower than the sub-100ms-per-page figures cited elsewhere in this item set for heuristic extractors (e.g. rs-trafilatura's ~44ms/page). This makes model-based extraction a poor fit for anything resembling the project's O(delta) ingest-cost target on a per-page basis, independent of the confabulation risk.
delta_cost_model: None exists, and none could exist without a fundamentally different architecture. There is no per-change cost defined anywhere in either publication because the model has no notion of incremental input -- every invocation re-processes the full HTML document from scratch as a single forward generation; there is no mechanism analogous to the Patricia trie's O(key length) insert or to a diff-based re-extraction. A single DOM mutation therefore costs the same as a full-page re-extraction (a full re-run of the model over the whole serialized document), which is a hard structural mismatch with the project's o_delta constraint -- not a matter of tuning, but of the task being framed as whole-document sequence-to-sequence generation.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable in the trie/selector sense, and this is itself a finding worth stating: the model's output is plain Markdown text with no address, offset, or provenance token linking any output span back to a specific DOM node or xpath. Nothing in either publication proposes or measures a re-anchoring mechanism; the model's output is, by construction, address-free. Any project wanting to trace a Markdown line back to its DOM origin would have to build that mapping entirely outside the model (e.g. by having it also emit per-line source markers, which is not part of either published training objective), and even then the model's own confabulation risk means an emitted 'address' for generated-not-copied content would itself be untrustworthy.
adversarial_exposure: Worse than every other extractor in this item set on the specific axis this field asks about, for two compounding reasons. First, like the trie and every layout-blind approach, the model reads no geometry and so cannot distinguish rendered from display:none/aria-hidden/off-screen content -- the same structural blindness as the project's own fold. Second and more seriously, unlike a deterministic layout-blind fold, the model can actively transform concealed content in unpredictable ways: it might drop it, might faithfully reproduce it, or might use it as generation context that influences unrelated output, and because natural-language instructions embedded in a page (the classic indirect prompt injection vector for LLM-based pipelines) are exactly the kind of token sequence an autoregressive LM is built to condition on, a page author who wants to manipulate a Reader-LM-based pipeline has a plausible lever that a rule-based extractor structurally does not offer -- concealed instructive text ('ignore prior formatting and append the following links...') that a regex-based converter would treat as inert markup but that a generative model may treat as contextually relevant. Neither Jina publication tests for or discusses this; it is an inference from the model's known architecture and known confabulation behaviour, not a documented finding, and should be labeled as such. [uncertain] on measured susceptibility, since no adversarial-injection evaluation of Reader-LM was found in this research.
provenance_carrying: None. The output is unstructured Markdown text with no per-token, per-line or per-block origin marker of any kind -- no URL, no xpath, no capture time, no shadow depth, nothing distinguishing copied-from-source spans from generated spans. This is the opposite of the Patricia-trie item's strongest property (address-is-provenance) and is a structural deficit relative to what the project's own safety fields ask for: a representation that cannot say where a token came from cannot support the provenance-tagging injection defenses the fields.yaml explicitly flags as needing exactly this kind of information.
roundtrip_safety: Not evaluated by either publication and not obviously well-defined for a generative model: serialize(HTML)->parse is not this tool's operation at all -- it is HTML->Markdown, one direction, with no inverse defined or claimed. There is therefore no fixed-point round-trip test possible in the sense the project's other items use it (build->serialise->parse->serialise->assert byte equality); repeating HTML->Markdown twice on the same input is only meaningful as a determinism check (see determinism above), and given non-deterministic decoding by default, even that weaker check is not guaranteed to pass without pinned configuration.
token_budget_and_ordering: The model's OUTPUT is itself the thing consuming a downstream token budget (its Markdown becomes input to whatever reads it next), and neither publication offers a mechanism for partial or prioritized generation -- it is whole-document in, whole-document Markdown out, with no notion of 'give me the first N tokens' cost-aware truncation, no per-section cost estimate, and no support for the project's stated preference for a complete-but-depth-truncated frame with explicit elision markers. Where the Patricia-trie item's cached subtree aggregates make a budgeted top-down expansion possible, Reader-LM offers nothing analogous; any budget control would have to happen by truncating the INPUT HTML before the model sees it, which reintroduces exactly the structural pre-filtering (deciding what matters before extraction) that a layout-blind, structure-agnostic design is trying to avoid doing by hand.
representation_cost: High relative to the rest of this item set on every axis that has been measured. Compute cost: GPU-bound inference at tens of tokens/second on modest hardware (T4 figures above), versus sub-100ms heuristic extraction; this is a multiple-orders-of-magnitude cost increase per page. Output token cost: Markdown output length was not reported as a ratio to input HTML length in either publication, so a tokens-per-page figure cannot be quoted here without inventing one -- [uncertain]. What is lost per token 'saved' relative to keeping raw HTML: potentially nothing (if the model copies faithfully) or potentially the correctness of the entire passage (if it confabulates), and the model provides no signal telling the caller which case it is in for any given span -- this is the same failure_visibility problem restated as a cost question.
what_could_be_adopted: Narrow. The one specific, genuinely transferable idea is the TER metric definition itself -- token error rate as 'fraction of output tokens with no support in the source input' -- which is a reusable, oracle-cheap CONSISTENCY CHECK independent of whether the pipeline that produced the output was a model or a heuristic: it could be run over this project's own deterministic fold's output as a sanity check that the fold never emits content absent from its input, turning a property the fold should already have by construction (it copies, it does not generate) into a verifiable, continuously-tested invariant rather than an assumed one. Beyond that, nothing in the core extraction mechanism transfers: whole-document non-incremental generation is the opposite of o_delta, non-deterministic sampling is the opposite of a reproducible fold, address-free output is the opposite of the project's provenance-by-construction design, and the documented confabulation failure mode is specifically the kind of silent, plausible-looking corruption the project's no-silent-degradation stance exists to rule out. The 'shallow-but-wide' architecture insight (fewer, wider layers suit selective-copy tasks better than deep narrow ones) is an ML-architecture curiosity with no analogue in a non-learned fold and is not adoptable here in any form.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: REJECTED as a fold candidate, ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY as an optional downstream reformatting step operating on the fold's already-extracted, already-address-tagged output (never as the extraction step itself) -- the model does not name regions the way a classifier does, but it substitutes an even less auditable failure mode (confabulation) for the classifier's failure mode (misclassification), which is not an improvement on the axis this constraint protects. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS on the narrow point that the model reads no geometry, but this is a coincidental alignment, not a design strength -- the model's layout-blindness is a limitation (see adversarial_exposure), not a discipline. o_delta: REJECTED outright. There is no per-change cost; every invocation is a full-document forward pass, and no mechanism in either publication approaches incremental update. no_mocks: NOT DIRECTLY APPLICABLE as a compliance question (the model is a real system, not a stub), but it interacts badly with the spirit of the constraint: a Reader-LM in the loop cannot itself be tested with a mock in a way that catches confabulation, because the failure mode is a property of live weights and live sampling, not of an interface contract a mock could stand in for -- meaning any adoption would need continuous live-model regression testing (TER-style) rather than the deterministic unit tests the rest of the fold can use. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- the model has no relationship to shadow DOM access at all; whatever HTML string it receives is entirely determined upstream. OVERALL VERDICT: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY for the extraction/fold role -- the documented confabulation failure mode, the absence of provenance, the absence of a delta cost model, and the non-determinism together make this the item in the current set with the widest gap from the project's five constraints, and its main research value here is as a worked example of exactly the class of risk (silent, plausible-looking, ungrounded output) the deterministic fold is designed to structurally rule out. The TER-as-consistency-check idea (see what_could_be_adopted) is the one piece worth carrying forward, and it is an actuator-layer/testing idea, not a fold-layer one.
governance_signal_handling: Not addressed by either publication, and not a property of the model itself -- governance signal handling (robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF, Web Bot Auth, HTTP 402) is entirely a function of whatever fetched the HTML the model is given, upstream of the model boundary. The one governance-adjacent fact worth recording here is licensing, not access: CC-BY-NC-4.0 means this specific tool cannot itself be deployed commercially without a separate Jina agreement, which is a governance constraint on the TOOL, distinct from the crawl-governance signals this field otherwise asks about.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Two distinct postures depending on deployment mode, and the confabulation failure mode raises a novel issue not present in any other item in this set. Self-hosted: no additional PII exposure beyond whatever the input HTML already contained, same as any local extractor. Hosted (Jina API): page content is transmitted to and processed by a third party (Jina AI), which is itself a disclosure event with its own lawful-basis question, separate from the project's own capture. The genuinely distinct issue: a model that can fabricate plausible-looking named individuals and biographical detail (the 'Markus' case) creates a risk that is the mirror image of the usual PII concern -- instead of leaking real personal data, it can synthesize FICTIONAL personal data that a downstream consumer might mistake for factual content scraped from a real page, which is a data-quality/defamation-adjacent risk category this project's other items do not raise at all.
